text:
ConocoPhillips fell 3.3% today as U.S. crude oil prices dropped sharply, sliding below $100 a barrel after the Trump administration signaled openness to negotiations with Iran at the UN. Oil traders are reassessing geopolitical risk: while Middle East tensions remain elevated—with the Strait of Hormuz still closed, Saudi infrastructure under attack, and the kingdom's key East-West pipeline shut down—the prospect of diplomatic talks has eased immediate fears of supply disruption, at least temporarily. A major oil producer's stock typically moves with the price of the commodity it sells, and a $7-per-barrel decline in U.S. crude in a day is a significant headwind.

The broader picture shows this stock has given back all its gains from earlier in the month, falling 5% over two weeks as the market grapples with conflicting signals: real supply constraints (Saudi pipeline down, Asian buyers scrambling) weighed against de-escalation hopes that could ease those constraints. For an integrated oil company, lower crude prices directly compress profit margins, which is why the stock has tracked the oil selloff so closely.
